The K-value from subgroup-specific net benefits

k_value.Rd

The K-value of Wang et al. for two subgroups, from their differences in net benefit (e.g. published values), without patient data: the critical ratio \(k_1/k_2\) of the incremental utility of a true positive relative to a false negative (\(a - c\)) at which population-level net benefit and population utility start to favour different strategies, $$K = -\frac{n_2 \Delta NB_2}{n_1 \Delta NB_1}.$$ It is defined when the two \(\Delta NB\) have opposite signs. When \(k_1 > k_2\), population net benefit and utility favour different strategies if \(k_1/k_2 > K\); when \(k_1 < k_2\), if \(k_1/k_2 < K\). With patient data, summary() of a result of nb_val() with subgroup gives the same check at every threshold.

Usage

k_value(diff_nb, shares = NULL, k = NULL)

Arguments

diff_nb

The difference in net benefit between the model and the comparator (the same strategy in both subgroups) in each of the two subgroups, named by subgroup, e.g. c(Men = -0.0016, Women = 0.00345).

shares

Optional relative sizes of the two subgroups, named like diff_nb. Default: equal.

k

Optional \(a - c\) of each subgroup (e.g. the relative risk reductions of the treatment), named like diff_nb.

Value

An object of class voipred_k_value, a list with diff_nb, shares, K (NA when the signs are the same), k and consistent (with k: whether population net benefit and population utility favour the same strategy), printed as a short report.

References

Wang J, Wang KZ, Van Calster B, van Geloven N, Steyerberg E, Wynants L. Population-level decision curve analysis may mislead the evaluation of prediction model usefulness under subgroup utility heterogeneity.

Examples

# SCORE2 at a 3% threshold (the case study of Wang et al.)
k_value(c(Men = -0.0016, Women = 0.00345))
#> Subgroup difference in net benefit (diff_NB): Men -0.00160, Women 0.00345 (opposite signs)
#> Shares: Men 50%, Women 50%
#> K-value (k_Men / k_Women): 2.156
#> Population NB and population utility favour different strategies if k_Men / k_Women is beyond 2.156 (above it when k_Men > k_Women, below it when k_Men < k_Women).
k_value(c(Men = -0.0016, Women = 0.00345), k = c(Men = 0.28, Women = 0.15))
#> Subgroup difference in net benefit (diff_NB): Men -0.00160, Women 0.00345 (opposite signs)
#> Shares: Men 50%, Women 50%
#> K-value (k_Men / k_Women): 2.156
#> Population NB and population utility favour different strategies if k_Men / k_Women is beyond 2.156 (above it when k_Men > k_Women, below it when k_Men < k_Women).
#> With k: k_Men / k_Women = 1.867, so population NB and population utility favour the same strategy.
k_value(c(Men = -0.0016, Women = 0.00345), k = c(Men = 0.28, Women = 0.12))
#> Subgroup difference in net benefit (diff_NB): Men -0.00160, Women 0.00345 (opposite signs)
#> Shares: Men 50%, Women 50%
#> K-value (k_Men / k_Women): 2.156
#> Population NB and population utility favour different strategies if k_Men / k_Women is beyond 2.156 (above it when k_Men > k_Women, below it when k_Men < k_Women).
#> With k: k_Men / k_Women = 2.333, so population NB and population utility favour different strategies.
